title: Oil and gas operators turn to AI and integrated automation to cut costs, speed up delivery
summary: In an interview with Zawya Projects, Sebastien Grau, Global Industry VP for Process Industries, Rockwell Automation said integrated power, process and safety systems, combined with digital twins and AI-assisted engineering, could help contractors reduce...

contentHtml:
Oil and gas operators are increasingly adopting integrated power, process and safety systems alongside artificial intelligence (AI) and digital simulation technologies to accelerate project delivery, reduce engineering costs and improve operational efficiency, according to a top executive of US-based Rockwell Automation.

Sebastien Grau, Global Industry VP for Process Industries told Zawya Projects that the shift is creating opportunities for technology providers to support engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractors and project owners, particularly in greenfield developments where digital systems can be incorporated from the initial design stage. 

He said the company's integrated automation platform allows process control, electrical power management and safety systems to be engineered and tested within a common software environment, reducing the need to develop and integrate separate systems.

“For example, to do the settings of a drive, you use the same software you use to program your Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs),” he said. “Every R&D development happens on the same platform — for process, power, and even safety.”  

He added that the company’s Logix SIS safety system is being offered as part its integrated control and safety system offering. 

Rockwell's Logix Echo and Emulate3D technologies enable engineers to simulate control systems and equipment behaviour, including responses to unexpected operating conditions, within a virtual environment.

Grau claimed that these capabilities could accelerate certain implementation activities by a factor of 100 compared with conventional approaches, although he did not provide a project-specific benchmark.

Greenfield project opportunities

The Rockwell Automation executive said greenfield projects offer greater opportunities to capture the benefits of integrated engineering because digital twins, control systems and simulation models can be developed together from the outset.

"I believe we can help end users and EPCs much more there — to fast-track their design, helping with design tools, helping with simulation and emulation," he said. “The digital twin is built at the very beginning.”

He added that model predictive control (MPC), a closed loop automation which traditionally required six months to a year of data generation before being efficient, can now be deployed on a fast-track basis. Simulation and emulation tools can generate data under different operating and environmental conditions before commissioning.

Grau also outlined an AI-assisted engineering approach via Factory Talk Conductor, in which natural-language instructions are used to define the system, generate three-dimensional plant models, simulate operating conditions and develop control software.

“We first build the digital twin: speed, pumps, flow simulation, temperature, pressure, tank management. Once that's done, you click on the button and it generates 100 percent of the code. You press another button, you can generate all the human-machine interface (HMI) and supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) screens.

He added that the approach brings together activities that were segregated and undertaken through separate tools.

 Brownfield modernisation

While greenfield projects offer greater scope for integrated design, Grau said existing oil and gas facilities also present significant opportunities for automation upgrades.

Many operators remain dependent on distributed control systems (DCS) installed decades ago, creating challenges around software upgrades, interoperability and dependence on individual technology suppliers.

He said customers are increasingly exploring open process automation and software-defined architectures to improve flexibility and reduce dependence on proprietary systems.

"How can I become more independent from a forced platform, a DCS platform? Thirty, thirty-five years with the same system, and I cannot move," Grau said, describing a concern among operators.

However, he acknowledged that oil and gas companies are cautious about adopting new technologies because failures in process control, fire and gas detection or emergency shutdown systems can have serious consequences for production, equipment and personnel safety.

“They don't want two separate platforms for process and for power and for safety. That's why the concept of ICSS came around,” he said.

The bigger shift was towards open process automation and software-defined architectures that could accommodate equipment and technologies from multiple suppliers.

Operators were increasingly testing these technologies through proof-of-concept (POC), Minimum viable Products (MVP) projects and limited deployments on less critical assets before considering wider implementation, he added.

He pointed out that Rockwell works extensively through system integrators, with approximately 90 percent of its business delivered through partners. The company has around 10 to 12 highly capable system integrators in the Middle East.

Cybersecurity and open systems

Grau said growing demand for open and interoperable automation systems does not necessarily mean increased cybersecurity risk, provided appropriate safeguards are implemented.

He argued that closed systems can also be vulnerable because operators depend on a limited number of vendors to identify and address security weaknesses.

He says one cannot argue that Information Technology (IT) is more or less vulnerable than operational technology (OT).

“If you are in a SDA environment, you are more in an IT environment. We apply cybersecurity protocols well proven on the IT side onto the OT side, so the more OT opens up, the more we adapt best practices from one side to the other.” 

Rockwell is expanding its OT cybersecurity capabilities, including through Verve, which provides visibility into connected industrial assets and helps identify vulnerabilities and obsolete equipment.

“When you have a proper understanding of what is obsolete, you have a very deep understanding of what is vulnerable,” said Grau.

He said cybersecurity must be integrated into the design and operation of automation systems as industrial facilities become increasingly connected.

Edge AI 

Grau identified the deployment of AI closer to industrial equipment as another area of growing investment.

Traditionally, industrial AI applications have relied on data collected from multiple systems and processed through centralised analytics platforms.

“Securitisation of the data was always an issue if you wanted to work on the cloud,” he pointed out, adding that a workaround was having private clouds, which often wasn’t as powerful as the centralised analytic platforms.

“What we see today is that we are securing the data by bringing the edge computer down to the process, and having a Software-Defined Automation (SDA) platform, which gives the flexibility to put AI or machine learning very close to the edge or down to the PLC level.”

For example, by merging condition monitoring with reading of the current signature of the compressor motor on an edge computer, one could generate an AI model that is the most advanced predictive maintenance for that asset. And the data generated is clean, according to Grau.

“It's contextualising and cleaning the data at the root of generation. You don't need a hundred data scientists cleaning data,” he said.

He said this also allows advanced process control applications to operate closer to individual assets.

However, analytics would continue to be required to do Root-Cause Analysis, identify relationships and operational problems across multiple assets, he added.

Grau said SDA can combine PLC, remote input/output, control, and computing functions into a single DIN-rail-mounted device. 

“You have computer capability, power, and memory to be able to run clear, dedicated applications and workflow on the same form factor,” he said, adding that this approach reduces both hardware and computing costs.

Opportunities outlook

Grau pointed to investment in gas transportation and export infrastructure in North America, alongside offshore developments in Brazil and the Gulf of Mexico as key opportunities for integrated automation technologies.

For example, the absence of midstream infrastructure has forced many gas producers in the Permian basin to shut wells despite super-high domestic demand since they don’t have means to transport the gas for self-use, sale and export.

He said there is growing interest in upstream exploration in Africa, Latin America and Indonesia and offshore developments – floating production storage and offloading (FPSO) – in Brazil and the Gulf of Mexico/America.

“In the last two quarters, the bottom lines of IOCs in the US have skyrocketed, so we see good momentum,” said Grau.  

In the Middle East, he said improving extraction efficiency and reducing operating costs at mature oil and gas fields would be particularly important.

He said traditional extraction methods and the limited digitalisation of ageing oil and gas fields are hindering the effective utilisation of data to improve performance.

Looking ahead, Grau expects AI, robotics, SDA and cybersecurity to support a broader transition towards autonomous operations as oil and gas companies prioritise workforce safety in hazardous environments and manage shortage of talent.

He said these four factors drive the shift from deterministic control systems — where an automation engineer would write code predicting what can happen or instructing the process how to behave — to an autonomous system that adapts itself to any type of variable environments without pre-defined code.

He said major international and national oil companies are developing business cases and testing technologies that could eventually be deployed across multiple assets.

Rockwell is increasingly using approximately 12-week implementation cycles to develop and validate minimum viable products before committing to larger deployments.

"We do a twelve-week implementation of many of the things we do, to create the MVP," Grau said.

"When you succeed, those twelve-week successes have to be implemented at scale. And that is what we are doing more and more.”

(Reporting by Anoop Menon; Editing by Dennis Daniel)
